## Introduction

MaxDiff, also called **Best-Worst Scaling**, is a survey method for measuring relative preference. On each screen, a respondent sees a small set of items and chooses the one they like most and the one they like least. This is useful because people are usually better at making trade-offs than giving stable 1-to-10 ratings.

In this assignment, the items are the 10 core MSBA classes at UCSD Rady. I will estimate class preferences in three ways:

1. A simple **counts analysis**
2. A **multinomial logit (MNL)** model fit by **maximum likelihood**
3. The same MNL model fit by **Bayesian methods** with Metropolis-Hastings

I expected the three methods to agree on the broad ranking, especially at the top and bottom. That is mostly what happens. The main differences show up in how each method describes uncertainty and how directly it models the choice process.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from IPython.display import display
from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import logsumexp

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", context="talk")
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 140
plt.rcParams["axes.titlesize"] = 16
plt.rcParams["axes.labelsize"] = 12


def show_table(table_df, caption, formats=None):
    styler = table_df.style.hide(axis="index")
    if formats is not None:
        styler = styler.format(formats)
    else:
        styler = styler.format(precision=3)
    styler = styler.set_caption(caption).set_table_styles(
        [
            {
                "selector": "caption",
                "props": [
                    ("caption-side", "top"),
                    ("font-size", "1.05em"),
                    ("font-weight", "bold"),
                    ("text-align", "left"),
                ],
            },
            {
                "selector": "th",
                "props": [
                    ("background-color", "#EEF3F8"),
                    ("font-weight", "bold"),
                ],
            },
            {
                "selector": "td, th",
                "props": [
                    ("padding", "8px 10px"),
                    ("border", "1px solid #D8E0EA"),
                ],
            },
        ]
    )
    display(styler)


raw = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_design_and_choices.csv")
labels = pd.read_csv("maxdiff_item_labels.csv").iloc[:, :2].copy()
labels.columns = ["item", "label"]

short_label_map = {
    1: "AI Math",
    2: "SQL",
    3: "MFO",
    4: "Large Data",
    5: "Biz Analytics",
    6: "Consulting",
    7: "Customer An.",
    8: "Capstone",
    9: "Marketing An.",
    10: "BI Systems",
}

palette = {
    1: "#4C78A8",
    2: "#F58518",
    3: "#E45756",
    4: "#72B7B2",
    5: "#54A24B",
    6: "#EECA3B",
    7: "#B279A2",
    8: "#FF9DA6",
    9: "#9D755D",
    10: "#BAB0AC",
}

# Keep the rows that match the 10-class assignment design.
candidate = raw[raw["Item"].between(1, 10)].copy()
task_checks = (
    candidate.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"])
    .agg(
        n_rows=("Item", "size"),
        n_best=("Response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
        n_worst=("Response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
        n_zero=("Response", lambda x: (x == 0).sum()),
        n_unique_items=("Item", "nunique"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

valid_tasks = task_checks.query(
    "n_rows == 4 and n_best == 1 and n_worst == 1 and n_zero == 2 and n_unique_items == 4"
)[["Record ID", "Task"]]

df = candidate.merge(valid_tasks, on=["Record ID", "Task"], how="inner").copy()

N = df["Record ID"].nunique()
T = int(valid_tasks.groupby("Record ID")["Task"].nunique().mode().iloc[0])
J_task = int(df.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"]).size().mode().iloc[0])
J_total = int(labels["item"].nunique())

raw_clean_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Metric": [
            "Task IDs in raw export",
            "Valid 4-row MaxDiff tasks kept",
            "Rows dropped",
        ],
        "Value": [
            int(task_checks.shape[0]),
            int(valid_tasks.shape[0]),
            int(raw.shape[0] - df.shape[0]),
        ],
    }
)

overview_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Respondents": [N],
        "Tasks per respondent": [T],
        "Items shown per task": [J_task],
        "Total classes in study": [J_total],
        "Valid MaxDiff tasks": [valid_tasks.shape[0]],
    }
)

exposure_table = (
    df.groupby("Item")
    .agg(Times_shown=("Item", "size"))
    .reset_index()
    .merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")
    .assign(Short=lambda x: x["Item"].map(short_label_map))
    .sort_values("Item")
    [["Item", "Short", "label", "Times_shown"]]
)

counts_df = (
    df.groupby("Item")
    .agg(
        shown=("Item", "size"),
        best=("Response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
        worst=("Response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
    )
    .reindex(range(1, 11))
)
counts_df["pct_best"] = counts_df["best"] / counts_df["shown"]
counts_df["pct_worst"] = counts_df["worst"] / counts_df["shown"]
counts_df["score"] = counts_df["pct_best"] - counts_df["pct_worst"]

# Bootstrap CIs for the counts score by resampling respondents.
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
respondent_ids = df["Record ID"].unique()
respondent_groups = {rid: g for rid, g in df.groupby("Record ID")}
B = 600
boot_scores = np.empty((B, 10))

for b in range(B):
    sample_ids = rng.choice(respondent_ids, size=len(respondent_ids), replace=True)
    sample = pd.concat([respondent_groups[rid] for rid in sample_ids], ignore_index=True)
    tmp = (
        sample.groupby("Item")
        .agg(
            shown=("Item", "size"),
            best=("Response", lambda x: (x == 1).sum()),
            worst=("Response", lambda x: (x == -1).sum()),
        )
        .reindex(range(1, 11))
    )
    boot_scores[b] = (tmp["best"] / tmp["shown"] - tmp["worst"] / tmp["shown"]).to_numpy()

counts_df["score_low"] = np.quantile(boot_scores, 0.025, axis=0)
counts_df["score_high"] = np.quantile(boot_scores, 0.975, axis=0)

counts_table = (
    counts_df.reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"index": "Item"})
    .merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")
    .assign(Short=lambda x: x["Item"].map(short_label_map))
    .sort_values("score", ascending=False)
    [["Item", "Short", "label", "shown", "best", "worst", "pct_best", "pct_worst", "score"]]
    .rename(
        columns={
            "shown": "Times shown",
            "best": "Times best",
            "worst": "Times worst",
            "pct_best": "% best",
            "pct_worst": "% worst",
            "score": "Score",
        }
    )
)

# Build one row per valid MaxDiff task.
task_rows = []
for (rid, task), g in df.groupby(["Record ID", "Task"]):
    shown = g.sort_values("Position")["Item"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
    best = int(g.loc[g["Response"] == 1, "Item"].iloc[0])
    worst = int(g.loc[g["Response"] == -1, "Item"].iloc[0])
    task_rows.append((rid, task, *shown, best, worst))

task_df = pd.DataFrame(
    task_rows,
    columns=["Record ID", "Task", "i1", "i2", "i3", "i4", "best", "worst"],
)

shown_mat = task_df[["i1", "i2", "i3", "i4"]].to_numpy(dtype=int)
best_items = task_df["best"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
worst_items = task_df["worst"].to_numpy(dtype=int)
remaining_mat = np.array(
    [row[row != b] for row, b in zip(shown_mat, best_items)],
    dtype=int,
)

J = 10
K = J - 1
free_items = np.arange(2, 11)
free_pos = {item: idx for idx, item in enumerate(free_items)}


def expand_beta(beta_free):
    beta = np.zeros(J + 1)
    beta[2:] = beta_free
    return beta


def loglik(beta_free):
    beta = expand_beta(beta_free)
    util_shown = beta[shown_mat]
    ll_best = beta[best_items] - logsumexp(util_shown, axis=1)
    util_remaining = -beta[remaining_mat]
    ll_worst = -beta[worst_items] - logsumexp(util_remaining, axis=1)
    return float(np.sum(ll_best + ll_worst))


def negloglik(beta_free):
    return -loglik(beta_free)


def grad_negloglik(beta_free):
    beta = expand_beta(beta_free)
    grad = np.zeros(K)

    for shown, best, worst, remaining in zip(
        shown_mat, best_items, worst_items, remaining_mat
    ):
        p_best = np.exp(beta[shown] - logsumexp(beta[shown]))
        p_worst = np.exp(-beta[remaining] - logsumexp(-beta[remaining]))

        for item, prob in zip(shown, p_best):
            if item != 1:
                grad[free_pos[item]] += prob
        if best != 1:
            grad[free_pos[best]] -= 1

        for item, prob in zip(remaining, p_worst):
            if item != 1:
                grad[free_pos[item]] -= prob
        if worst != 1:
            grad[free_pos[worst]] += 1

    return grad


def hess_negloglik(beta_free):
    beta = expand_beta(beta_free)
    hess = np.zeros((K, K))

    for shown, remaining in zip(shown_mat, remaining_mat):
        p_best = np.exp(beta[shown] - logsumexp(beta[shown]))
        idx_best = [free_pos[item] for item in shown if item != 1]
        probs_best = np.array([p_best[list(shown).index(item)] for item in shown if item != 1])
        hess[np.ix_(idx_best, idx_best)] += np.diag(probs_best) - np.outer(
            probs_best, probs_best
        )

        p_worst = np.exp(-beta[remaining] - logsumexp(-beta[remaining]))
        idx_worst = [free_pos[item] for item in remaining if item != 1]
        probs_worst = np.array(
            [p_worst[list(remaining).index(item)] for item in remaining if item != 1]
        )
        hess[np.ix_(idx_worst, idx_worst)] += np.diag(probs_worst) - np.outer(
            probs_worst, probs_worst
        )

    return hess


mle_result = minimize(
    negloglik,
    np.zeros(K),
    method="trust-ncg",
    jac=grad_negloglik,
    hess=hess_negloglik,
)

beta_hat_free = mle_result.x
beta_hat_full = np.r_[0.0, beta_hat_free]
se_hat = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(hess_negloglik(beta_hat_free))))
share_hat = np.exp(beta_hat_full) / np.exp(beta_hat_full).sum()

mle_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Item": np.arange(1, 11),
            "Beta (MLE)": beta_hat_full,
            "SE": np.r_[np.nan, se_hat],
            "Share of preference": share_hat,
        }
    )
    .merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")
    .assign(Short=lambda x: x["Item"].map(short_label_map))
    .sort_values("Share of preference", ascending=False)
    [["Item", "Short", "label", "Beta (MLE)", "SE", "Share of preference"]]
)

# Bayesian MNL with a weakly informative N(0, 10I) prior on the free betas.
prior_var = 10.0


def log_post(beta_free):
    prior = -0.5 * np.sum(beta_free**2 / prior_var) - 0.5 * K * np.log(2 * np.pi * prior_var)
    return loglik(beta_free) + prior


def mh_sampler(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=2026):
    rng_local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = beta0.copy()
    lp = log_post(beta)
    draws = np.empty((n_iter, len(beta0)))
    accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_star = beta + rng_local.normal(0, step, size=len(beta0))
        lp_star = log_post(beta_star)

        if np.log(rng_local.random()) < lp_star - lp:
            beta = beta_star
            lp = lp_star
            accept += 1

        draws[t] = beta

    return draws, accept / n_iter


pilot_steps = [0.06, 0.07, 0.08, 0.09]
pilot_rows = []
for idx, step in enumerate(pilot_steps):
    _, acc_rate = mh_sampler(beta_hat_free, n_iter=2000, step=step, seed=300 + idx)
    pilot_rows.append({"Proposal step": step, "Acceptance rate": acc_rate})
pilot_table = pd.DataFrame(pilot_rows)

step_candidates = pilot_table.loc[
    pilot_table["Acceptance rate"].between(0.25, 0.40), "Proposal step"
]
chosen_step = 0.08

draws_free, accept_rate = mh_sampler(beta_hat_free, n_iter=20000, step=chosen_step, seed=2026)
burn_in = 5000
post_free = draws_free[burn_in:]
post_full = np.column_stack([np.zeros(len(post_free)), post_free])
share_draws = np.exp(post_full) / np.exp(post_full).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

posterior_mean = post_full.mean(axis=0)
posterior_sd = post_full.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
posterior_low = np.quantile(post_full, 0.025, axis=0)
posterior_high = np.quantile(post_full, 0.975, axis=0)
posterior_share = share_draws.mean(axis=0)
posterior_share_low = np.quantile(share_draws, 0.025, axis=0)
posterior_share_high = np.quantile(share_draws, 0.975, axis=0)

bayes_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Item": np.arange(1, 11),
            "Posterior mean beta": posterior_mean,
            "CI low": posterior_low,
            "CI high": posterior_high,
            "Posterior mean share": posterior_share,
        }
    )
    .merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")
    .assign(Short=lambda x: x["Item"].map(short_label_map))
    .sort_values("Posterior mean share", ascending=False)
    [["Item", "Short", "label", "Posterior mean beta", "CI low", "CI high", "Posterior mean share"]]
)

comparison_table = (
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Item": np.arange(1, 11),
            "Counts score": counts_df["score"].to_numpy(),
            "MLE share": share_hat,
            "Bayes share": posterior_share,
        }
    )
    .merge(labels, left_on="Item", right_on="item")
    .assign(Short=lambda x: x["Item"].map(short_label_map))
)
comparison_table["Counts rank"] = comparison_table["Counts score"].rank(
    ascending=False, method="first"
).astype(int)
comparison_table["MLE rank"] = comparison_table["MLE share"].rank(
    ascending=False, method="first"
).astype(int)
comparison_table["Bayes rank"] = comparison_table["Bayes share"].rank(
    ascending=False, method="first"
).astype(int)
comparison_table = comparison_table.sort_values("MLE rank")[
    ["Item", "Short", "label", "Counts score", "Counts rank", "MLE share", "MLE rank", "Bayes share", "Bayes rank"]
]

trace_items = [9, 5, 6]
trace_labels = [short_label_map[i] for i in trace_items]
trace_df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Iteration": np.arange(1, draws_free.shape[0] + 1),
        trace_labels[0]: draws_free[:, trace_items[0] - 2],
        trace_labels[1]: draws_free[:, trace_items[1] - 2],
        trace_labels[2]: draws_free[:, trace_items[2] - 2],
    }
)
```

Those rows do not match the MaxDiff structure described in the homework template, so I keep only the valid 4-row MaxDiff tasks built from the 10 labeled classes.

## Counts Analysis

The counts approach is the fastest descriptive summary. For each class, I compute:

$$
\text{score}_j = \% \text{best}_j - \% \text{worst}_j
$$

If a class is often picked as best and rarely picked as worst, the score is high. If the opposite happens, the score is low.

```{python}
#| label: counts-table
show_table(
    counts_table,
    "Table 4. Counts analysis ranked from most preferred to least preferred.",
    {
        "Item": "{:,.0f}",
        "Times shown": "{:,.0f}",
        "Times best": "{:,.0f}",
        "Times worst": "{:,.0f}",
        "% best": "{:.1%}",
        "% worst": "{:.1%}",
        "Score": "{:.3f}",
    },
)
```


The story is already clear. **Marketing Analytics** is the strong favorite by a wide margin. The next group is **Business Analytics**, **Customer Analytics**, and **Large Data**. At the bottom, **Analytics Consulting** has the lowest score, followed by **Marketing/Finance/Operations** and **AI Math**.

The middle of the ranking is closer. **Capstone** and **SQL** are almost tied, so I would not read too much into their exact order from the counts method alone.

## From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices

The counts method is useful, but it does not model the choice process directly. The MNL model does.

For each task, suppose the screen shows four items, such as $\{a, b, c, d\}$. The model gives each item a utility coefficient $\beta_j$. Then the probability that item $b$ is chosen as **best** is

$$
P(\text{best} = b) = \frac{\exp(\beta_b)}{\exp(\beta_a) + \exp(\beta_b) + \exp(\beta_c) + \exp(\beta_d)}.
$$

After the best item is removed, the probability that item $c$ is chosen as **worst** from the remaining three is

$$
P(\text{worst} = c \mid \text{best} = b) =
\frac{\exp(-\beta_c)}{\exp(-\beta_a) + \exp(-\beta_c) + \exp(-\beta_d)}.
$$

So each MaxDiff task creates **two** MNL observations:

1. one best choice from the full set of 4 items
2. one worst choice from the remaining set of 3 items

There is one identification issue. If we add the same constant to every $\beta_j$, the soft-max probabilities do not change. So only **9** free parameters are identified. I fix **item 1 (AI Math)** as the reference and set $\beta_1 = 0$.

```{python}
#| label: task-reshape
#| echo: true
task_df = pd.DataFrame(
    task_rows,
    columns=["Record ID", "Task", "i1", "i2", "i3", "i4", "best", "worst"],
)

task_df.head()
```

That task-level structure is much easier to use inside the likelihood function.

## MNL via Maximum Likelihood

For each task, the log-likelihood contribution is:

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) =
\sum_{\text{tasks}}
\left[
\beta_{j_b^*}
- \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown}} \exp(\beta_j)
- \beta_{j_w^*}
- \log \sum_{j \in \text{shown} \setminus \{j_b^*\}} \exp(-\beta_j)
\right].
$$

Here, $j_b^*$ is the best item and $j_w^*$ is the worst item.

```{python}
#| label: mle-functions
#| echo: true
def expand_beta(beta_free):
    beta = np.zeros(11)
    beta[2:] = beta_free
    return beta


def loglik(beta_free):
    beta = expand_beta(beta_free)
    util_shown = beta[shown_mat]
    ll_best = beta[best_items] - logsumexp(util_shown, axis=1)
    util_remaining = -beta[remaining_mat]
    ll_worst = -beta[worst_items] - logsumexp(util_remaining, axis=1)
    return float(np.sum(ll_best + ll_worst))


def negloglik(beta_free):
    return -loglik(beta_free)
```

I maximize the log-likelihood with `scipy.optimize.minimize()` and use the inverse Hessian for standard errors.

```{python}
#| label: mle-fit
#| echo: true
mle_result = minimize(
    negloglik,
    np.zeros(9),
    method="trust-ncg",
    jac=grad_negloglik,
    hess=hess_negloglik,
)
```

```{python}
#| label: mle-results-table
show_table(
    mle_table,
    "Table 5. MNL estimates from maximum likelihood.",
    {
        "Item": "{:,.0f}",
        "Beta (MLE)": "{:.3f}",
        "SE": "{:.3f}",
        "Share of preference": "{:.1%}",
    },
)
```

```{python}

    .sort_values("Share of preference", ascending=True)
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 6))
ax.barh(
    mle_plot["Short"],
    mle_plot["Share of preference"],
    color=[palette[i] for i in mle_plot["Item_num"]],
    edgecolor="white",

ax.set_xlabel("Share of preference")
ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.set_title("MNL shares of preference from maximum likelihood")

plt.show()
```

The MLE results are easy to read in share form. If all 10 classes were shown on one screen, the model predicts:

- **Marketing Analytics** would get about **28.4%** of choices
- **Business Analytics** would get about **11.7%**
- **Customer Analytics** would get about **10.7%**

The ranking is actually **identical** to the counts ranking in this dataset. That is a nice sign that the preference signal is strong. The middle classes are still close, but the overall order is stable.

One note about interpretation: **AI Math** has no standard error listed for its raw $\beta$ because I fixed it at zero as the reference item. That is just a normalization choice. It does **not** mean there is no uncertainty about AI Math's relative preference.

## MNL via Bayesian Estimation

Now I fit the same model with Bayes' rule:

$$
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \boldsymbol{y}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$

I use a weakly informative prior on the 9 free coefficients:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}_{2:10} \sim N(\mathbf{0}, 10I).
$$

Then I sample from the posterior with a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.

```{python}
#| label: bayes-code
#| echo: true
def log_post(beta_free):
    prior = -0.5 * np.sum(beta_free**2 / prior_var)
    prior -= 0.5 * len(beta_free) * np.log(2 * np.pi * prior_var)
    return loglik(beta_free) + prior


def mh_sampler(beta0, n_iter, step, seed=2026):
    rng_local = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    beta = beta0.copy()
    lp = log_post(beta)
    draws = np.empty((n_iter, len(beta0)))
    accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        beta_star = beta + rng_local.normal(0, step, size=len(beta0))
        lp_star = log_post(beta_star)

        if np.log(rng_local.random()) < lp_star - lp:
            beta = beta_star
            lp = lp_star
            accept += 1

        draws[t] = beta

    return draws, accept / n_iter
```

I tried a few proposal step sizes on short pilot chains and chose one that landed inside the suggested acceptance-rate range.

```{python}
#| label: pilot-tuning-table
show_table(
    pilot_table,
    "Table 6. Pilot tuning for the Metropolis proposal step size.",
    {"Proposal step": "{:.3f}", "Acceptance rate": "{:.1%}"},
)
```

The step size **0.08** worked well, so I used it in the main run. I then ran **20,000 iterations** and dropped the first **5,000** as burn-in. The final acceptance rate was **28.2%**.

```{python}
#| label: trace-plots
#| out-width: 86%
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 7), sharex=True)

for ax, label in zip(axes, trace_labels):
    ax.plot(trace_df["Iteration"], trace_df[label], color="#4C78A8", linewidth=0.6)
    ax.axvline(burn_in, color="#E45756", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set_ylabel(label)

axes[-1].set_xlabel("Iteration")
fig.suptitle("Trace plots for three MCMC parameters", y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

These traces look like the kind of "fuzzy caterpillar" we want. I do not see a long drift after burn-in, which suggests the chain is exploring a stable posterior region.

The Bayesian results are very close to the MLE results. The posterior mean shares are almost the same, and the posterior uncertainty is also similar to the classical standard errors. The only visible ranking difference is that **SQL** and **Capstone** swap places, which makes sense because they are extremely close in the middle of the pack.

The agreement here is strong.

- All three methods put **Marketing Analytics** in first place by a large margin.
- All three methods put **Analytics Consulting** in last place.
- The top four classes are the same across methods.
- The only tiny disagreement is around **SQL** and **Capstone**, where the posterior means are almost tied.

This is also a nice way to see what each method adds.

- The **counts analysis** is fast and intuitive, but it is only descriptive.
- The **MNL model** uses the actual choice mechanism, so every shown item contributes information through the soft-max probabilities.
- The **Bayesian version** makes uncertainty for derived quantities like preference shares very easy to report. I just transform every posterior draw and then summarize the distribution.

## Discussion

For a non-technical reader, the main substantive result is simple: students in this sample most prefer **Marketing Analytics**, and they also like **Business Analytics**, **Customer Analytics**, and **Large Data**. The least preferred classes are **Analytics Consulting**, **Marketing/Finance/Operations**, and **AI Math**.

Methodologically, the three tools are useful for slightly different jobs.

- **Counts** is great for a quick descriptive dashboard.
- **MLE MNL** is a good choice when I want a model-based ranking and a single classical estimate to report.
- **Bayesian MNL** is best when I care about uncertainty on simulated outcomes, preference shares, or future extensions like individual-level preference models.

There are also a few caveats. This was a self-selected sample of MSBA students, so the results may not generalize to all students. Preferences may also depend on timing, past coursework, concentration interests, and where a student is in the program.

If I had more time, I would do two next steps. First, I would estimate a **hierarchical Bayes** version to recover respondent-level heterogeneity. Second, I would explore whether first-year and second-year students rank these classes differently.
